Where the money is — the 10-spot paytable

The paytable is U-shaped: matching zero pays $5, and matching 5+ pays. Matching 1–4 pays nothing, and that dead zone swallows 89% of all draws. The single biggest source of expected value is the 0-match payout at 36%.

Which spot count is least bad

Ohio lets you pick 1 to 10 numbers per ticket, and each spot count runs its own paytable — so each has its own return. This site has run entirely on the 10-spot game so far, and 10-spot turns out to be the worst return of every multi-number spot count. Every figure below is copied straight from Ohio Lottery's own Odds & Payouts page, then independently recomputed here from the hypergeometric distribution and checked against their stated odds — the check column is that comparison, not a claim.

None of this changes the verdict — every spot count is still a losing bet, by design, forever — it only changes how much you lose per dollar wagered. 7-spot now has its own full page — predictions, algorithms, track record and all — linked from the dropdown above.

The 7-spot game

Same mechanism as 10-spot — 20 numbers drawn from 80, same draws, same archive — a different choice of how many numbers you mark and a different paytable. Matching 1 or 2 pays nothing; there is no 0-match consolation prize the way 10-spot has one, so the whole return comes from actually hitting something.

Predictions — locked before the draw

Each set below was written for a draw number higher than any draw we had seen, so the result did not exist when the prediction was recorded. Draw numbers rise with time, so target > known is the proof — shown on every row. Seven strategies run in parallel; the one in blue is the featured pick.

Track record

Every prediction that has since been drawn, scored. 10 numbers against twenty drawn from eighty means 2.5 hits is what chance delivers — that is the line to beat.

Generator sweep — searching for the algorithmstopped

A background process runs continuously, generating draws from known random-number generators and comparing them to real draws in true machine order. A match on order would be conclusive: one ordered draw carries 122.7 bits, so a hit could not be coincidence.

mean is the average number of balls matched out of 20. Chance gives exactly 5.0 (20×20÷80) — every row sits there. P(coincidence) is the probability that this many random tries would produce a result at least as good as that row’s best, computed from the hypergeometric distribution as 1−(1−p)N. Values near 100% mean “entirely expected”; anything under 5% would be worth investigating.

The draws, in the order they actually came out

The official archive sorts every draw ascending, which permanently destroys the sequence the machine produced — 61 bits per draw, thrown away and unrecoverable. This is the same draws in true pull order: big number is the ball, small number under it is when it came out. First ball out is outlined. Toggle to sorted to see what the official archive leaves you with.

Position matrix — where each ball lands, over a batch of draws

Every ball 1-80 down the side, every pull position 1-20 across the top. Each number keeps one fixed color everywhere on this page, so a row is that number's whole story across the batch: a cell lights up once for every time that ball came out in that position within the selected draws. Expected count per cell is printed below — most cells will be 0 or 1, because with 50-100 draws there just is not much data per cell yet.

Draw-order grid — one row per ticket, in the order it happened

The matrix above aggregates a batch into counts. This does not aggregate anything: row one is one ticket, in the exact order its 20 balls came out, oldest ticket in the batch at the top. Same colors as everywhere else on this page, so you can watch a number's color travel down the grid draw by draw instead of reading its number.

How each algorithm works

Every method on this page, what it does, and the actual expression it computes — taken straight from the code so the two cannot drift apart. Controls are marked; they read nothing from the lottery and exist so a real algorithm has something to beat.

When should an algorithm finally hit?

None of them has reached 8, 9 or 10 out of 10 yet. These are the dates by which each should — the point where it is a coin flip whether it has happened. Read the warning at the bottom before treating any of them as a countdown.

Archive coverage — what is actually collected

Every draw this archive holds, and every one it does not. Results and pull order are collected together from the same endpoint, so the two lines move as one. The bar tracks progress toward a full year of history; gaps are listed rather than smoothed over.

Draw order — which ball comes out when

The archive publishes every draw sorted, which throws away the sequence the machine actually produced. This table is built from the true pull order, collected separately and still filling in. Each position gets 75,018 samples spread over 80 balls, so chance alone puts 937.7 in every cell (sd 30.43) — and the biggest of 80 such cells lands near z = +2.5 without anything being wrong. Read the z column, not the counts.

Shadow game — play your own

Pick up to ten numbers and lock them in. Your picks are stored in this browser only, stamped with the newest draw at the moment you save, and scored only against draws after that point — the same no-lookahead rule the algorithms follow.
